overview: Two of the most common protozoan parasites causing gastrointestinal disease worldwide, distinguished by locomotion, invasiveness, and diagnostic appearance.
genZNote: Giardia has a face (and flagella) and just wants to float. E. histolytica actually invades.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: A flagellated protozoan that colonizes the small intestine, causing malabsorptive, non-bloody diarrhea.
aspects.valueB: An amoeba that can invade the colonic wall and spread to the liver, causing amoebic dysentery and abscesses.

aspects.label: Motility / Structure
aspects.valueA: Flagellated trophozoite with a distinctive "falling leaf" motility and two nuclei giving a classic "face" appearance.
aspects.valueB: Amoeboid trophozoite that moves via pseudopodia; can ingest red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis) when invasive.

aspects.label: Invasiveness
aspects.valueA: Non-invasive — attaches to the duodenal/jejunal mucosa via a ventral sucking disc without penetrating tissue.
aspects.valueB: Invasive — can penetrate the colonic mucosa and disseminate hematogenously, classically to the liver.

aspects.label: Clinical Presentation
aspects.valueA: Foul-smelling, greasy, non-bloody diarrhea with bloating and malabsorption (steatorrhea).
aspects.valueB: Bloody, mucus-containing diarrhea (amoebic dysentery) and potentially liver abscess.

aspects.label: Diagnostic Form in Stool
aspects.valueA: Trophozoites or cysts with 2-4 nuclei; antigen detection (ELISA) and PCR also used.
aspects.valueB: Trophozoites (with ingested RBCs if invasive) or cysts with up to 4 nuclei; antigen/PCR testing distinguishes it from non-pathogenic E. dispar.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueB: Amoeboid, invasive, can cause dysentery and liver abscess.
